# License

Ze is free software, licensed under the **GNU Affero General Public License,
version 3**.

Read the full text in the repository:
[LICENSE on GitHub](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/blob/main/LICENSE).

## What the AGPLv3 gives you

You are free to run Ze for any purpose, study how it works, modify it, and
share it, including modified versions. Those freedoms come with the usual
copyleft condition: anything you distribute that is derived from Ze must
itself be offered under the AGPLv3, with its source available.

## The network clause

The AGPL adds one obligation on top of the GPL. If you run a **modified** Ze
and let other people use it over a network, you have to make your modified
source available to those users. Running an unmodified Ze to route your own
traffic does not trigger this: the clause is about offering a changed version
as a service to others.

## Contributing

Contributions are accepted under a Contributor License Agreement that lets the
maintainer relicense the project in addition to the AGPL. You keep your
copyright, and Ze stays AGPLv3 for everyone. The [contribute page](../contribute/)
explains why, and the [contributor guide](../contribute/guide/) covers the
process.

If you have a licensing question that these notes do not answer, ask on
[Discord](https://discord.gg/T8s7CjPDne) or open an
[issue](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/issues).

### Page: Style guide.
https://ze-software.net/style-guide/

Design system

# Style guide.

The palette, components, and content rules this site follows -- so new pages stay consistent without re-deriving them from scratch.

## Palette: vivid candy claymation

Seven candy hues on a calm blush base.

Each hue ships four tones in `assets/site.css`: `-base` (the vivid candy color), `-deep` (text-safe dark), `-chip` (pill background), and `-tint` (card surface), plus a `-glow` for hue-tinted shadows. Never mix tones across hues on one component.

**Operate**

### Sky

`--sky-*`

Operator surfaces: SSH CLI, YANG configuration, web workbench, looking glass.

**Routing**

### Tangerine

`--tangerine-*`

Control plane: BGP engine, static routes, BFD, MRT, MPLS signaling.

**Services**

### Teal

`--teal-*`

Network services and data plane: VPN, BNG, firewall, interfaces, VPP, DNS.

**Automate**

### Grape

`--grape-*`

Programmability: plugins, APIs, MCP, ExaBGP migration, fleet management.

**Observe**

### Mint

`--mint-*`

Visibility and evidence: telemetry, health, diagnostics, testing proof.

**Secure**

### Pink

`--pink-*`

Security: SSH and RBAC, RPKI, TACACS+, audit trail, PKI store.

**Platform**

### Lemon

`--lemon-*`

Packaging and lifecycle: appliance and daemon targets, install, Docker, tunables.

### Neutrals and brand

`--bg / --text / --purple`

A flat dimmed-blush page background, deep plum text, grape-violet headings. Surfaces stay lighter than the page so cards float. Cards without a category stay blush-white.

## Color means category

On feature cards, color is information, never decoration.

A `cat-*` class on the card sets one accent hue for everything on it: the category chip, the title, the tech chips, the bullet markers, the bold words, and the hover glow. Do not color cards by position (`nth-child` cycling is banned for cards) and do not mix hues within one card. Decorative variety is fine only where order carries no meaning -- the homepage proof strip and audience trio.

**Routing**

### A well-formed card

`RFC 0000` `Tech`

- One hue, **every element**
- Chips name **technologies**
- Bullets state **facts**

**Platform**

### Mode chips

`Daemon only` `Example`

Features run in both daemon and appliance modes by default; a solid mode chip flags the exception. No "Both" pill on every card.

## The clay look

Molded, not just rounded with a drop shadow.

Every card-like surface (`.card`, `.button`, `.proof`, `.audience-card`, `.bird-card`, `.status-panel`, `.terminal-note`, `.closing`, the `.eyebrow` badge) carries `box-shadow: var(--clay)` plus a 2px white "sugar coat" border: an inset top highlight, a soft inset bottom shade, and a diffuse outer shadow. Hovers lift with a bouncy cubic-bezier and a hue-tinted glow. Add all of it to any new card-like component; don't invent a one-off shadow.

### With clay

This card. Notice the white coat, soft top highlight, and bottom depth even before hover.

### Without clay

Flat by comparison -- a plain bordered rectangle, no material feel.

## Page and card ornaments

Light linework, candy washes, and clay depth.

Page heroes and dispatch cards share one ornament language: translucent candy radial washes behind the content, thin concentric circle lines in an open corner, and optional masked grid lines for large hero surfaces. Keep ornaments low contrast and behind the text. Avoid filled balls, opaque blobs, heavy badges, or one-off shapes that fight the content.

Wide product comparison tables must keep the existing page filter and add product column controls so readers can hide projects they are not comparing. Keep those controls visible, keyboard-accessible, and honest: hiding a column changes the view only, never the source evidence or generated text.

Reuse `.journey-hero::before` for masked grid texture and `.journey-hero::after` for circle line treatment. Two-choice dispatch pages, including Compare, use `.compare-dispatch` cards with page-specific accent classes and the same concentric ring language.

### Hero pages

Use a soft candy wash, a masked grid, one ring ornament, and clay shadow. The content owns the foreground.

### Dispatch cards

Use one accent palette per choice and a light circle-line ornament. Do not use filled decorative balls.

### Generated pages

Start from existing components before adding CSS. If a page needs a new surface, document the rule here when the component ships.

## Component patterns to reuse

Don't invent new components for new pages -- these cover almost everything.

### .status-panel / .status-table

Two-column fact panel: prose on the left, labeled rows on the right. Used for lab pages' "Proves / Requires / Source" facts.

### .terminal-panel

Terminal (exact commands, candy traffic-light dots) + terminal-note (prerequisites, links) side by side. Used on every lab page and the homepage Try section.

### .cards / .card + cat-*

The feature-grid unit. A cat-* class sets the hue, .cat names the category, .chip pills tag technologies, .chip.mode flags Daemon/Appliance exceptions.

### .legend

Category filter buttons carrying the same cat-* classes as the cards they filter. One active category at a time; pressing again clears.

### .section-note

Full-width prose under a section head for anything longer than a sentence or two. The head's side text stays short so it never pushes the section's content down.

### Maturity tiers on cards

Shipped cards are solid clay. .card.experimental adds a dashed border and an "Experimental" status chip. .card.aspiration is a flat dashed blueprint whose title links to its pending spec in the main repo's plan/ directory.

### .doc-diagram

Full-width documentation figure with a clay frame, caption, and horizontal overflow that keeps detailed diagrams readable on narrow screens. Link the image to its standalone asset and keep a text equivalent below it.

### .md-content

Wraps Markdown rendered by the native `./le site build` pipeline: headings, tables, blockquotes, and code all match the rest of the site.

## Navigation rules

Top menu and right menu come from shared data; footer is a license line.

Use navigation to explain where the reader should go next, not as a dump of every page. The top mega-menu is the global map from `data/nav.json`. The right page menu is the local guide from `data/page-links.json`. The footer is the shared license line and publication stamp from `sitelib.footer_html`. Do not hand-code equivalent link lists in page bodies.

### Top mega-menu

Every multi-column dropdown must have a label at the top of each column. Group the top menu by reader job: Start, Evaluate, Docs, Examples, Reference, Project. Do not let a dropdown clip outside the viewport.

### Right menu

Use `.page-sidebar` for nearby choices, related evidence, and next steps. Add entries to `data/page-links.json`; `sitelib.patch_page_sidebar` injects the menu and the mobile layout.

### Reader path first

The right menu ranks what the reader likely wants next before external references. Research, debugging, comparison, and journey paths come before project homepages or vendor docs.

### External links

Every external link opens with `target="_blank"` and `rel="noopener"`. Never use a named target. Keep each external destination once in `data/page-links.json` instead of duplicating it in page bodies.

### Easy scanning

Prefer short labels, one-line descriptions, grouped links, and search boxes over long index pages. If a page becomes a catalogue, move details to per-item pages and keep the index as a route.

## Source and evidence rules

Claims, counts, navigation, and AI mirrors must be generated from source.

### Evidence for claims

Every claim about a feature, protocol, lab, benchmark, command, dependency, plugin, or quality gate must trace to a source file, Markdown source, JSON data file, script, generated binary output, or external reference.

### Generated data first

Do not hand-maintain lists that can come from Markdown or structured data. Use `data/*.json`, `../main/docs/*.md`, `go.mod`, registry extraction, YANG extraction, or live `bin/ze` output.

### Markdown mirrors

Every published page needs an `index.md` sibling for AI and text readers. Render it from the same Markdown or data as the HTML; only hand-authored pages may use the build step's HTML-to-Markdown extraction.

### `llms.txt`

`llms.txt` is generated from `data/nav.json` and live counts. Each entry links to the Markdown URL first, then the human web page. Never edit it by hand.

## Content rules

Agreed while building this site. Apply them to anything added later.

### Honesty about shortcomings

State where Ze is behind plainly and up front (see Compare) -- not buried in a table, not omitted.

### No fabrication

Every claim about what a feature or lab does traces to a real source file, doc, or script. If it can't be cited, don't state it as fact.

### No naming other network OSes

The BGP-daemon comparison table is an established, separate category. Beyond that, don't name competing full network operating systems in Ze's own copy.

### Daemon / Appliance labeling

Features run in both modes unless a .chip.mode says otherwise. Labs cards still tag modes explicitly with card-label pills, since labs are mode-specific.

### Write little in section heads

The text beside a title is one or two sentences, max. Longer verbiage moves to a .section-note under the head.

### Dedicated pages over a single page

New substantial content gets its own page and a top-nav or right-menu path, not another section bolted onto index.html.

### Markdown-sourced where it can be

Content that changes often, such as Compare, lives in a Markdown file rendered by `./le site build`, so updating it does not require hand-editing HTML tables.

### Page: Zeledon.
https://ze-software.net/zeledon/

Mascot

# Zeledon.

Ze's mascot, and the voice behind the weekly updates.

 ![Zeledon, the Ze bird mascot](https://ze-software.net/assets/zeledon.svg) Zeledon. `Who is Zeledon?`

Zeledon is Ze's mascot, and also the name for the voice that narrates the project. The weekly updates on this site's [blog](https://ze-software.net/blog/) and the posts in Ze's Discord `ze-news` channel are written as Zeledon, not as a person: they report what shipped, in plain language, without hype.

Zeledon never says "I built this". It says "Ze can now do this" -- the project speaks for itself, and whoever is behind the keyboard that week stays out of the sentence.

- [Weekly updates see Zeledon's voice in the archive](https://ze-software.net/blog/)
- [Discord: ze-news where updates post first](https://discord.gg/T8s7CjPDne)

## How Zeledon writes.

Confident and factual, never hype.

### Confident, not hypey

Reports what shipped. No "excited to announce", no "game-changing", no marketing adjectives. The audience is network engineers who can smell fluff.

### Third person, always

Zeledon is the narrator, not Thomas. Never "I did X" -- "Ze can now...", "shipped this week...".

### Only what shipped

Design and planning work goes under a clearly separate "Coming up" heading, phrased as started, not delivered. Nothing is claimed before it lands.

### No internal process language

The community sees features, not how they get built. No specs, review gates, or commit counts as a headline -- internal work gets translated into user-facing capability.

```
# from the Week of 2026-06-25 update
The installer's old busybox shell initrd is gone, replaced
by a single pure-Go PID-1 binary that boots the same way
over PXE or off USB/ISO media.
```

`What this isn't`

Not: "We're thrilled to announce a game-changing new installer, the culmination of months of work!" Zeledon reports the capability, not the effort behind it.

- [About](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/about): This section is the starting point if you have never heard of Ze, or if you have and want to know what is actually inside it.
- [What is Ze](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/what-is-ze): Ze turns a Linux server into a programmable network device.
- [Why Ze](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/why-ze): This is the long version of "what is this for, should I care".
- [Architecture](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/architecture): This page is the mental model.
- [History](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/history): Where Ze came from, and how it got to where it is now.
- [Status](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/status): Ze is in early active development.

### First Steps

- [First Steps](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/first-steps): This section takes you from an empty Linux box to a Ze daemon with its first BGP peer up.
- [Install](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/install): You build Ze from source.
- [Docker](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/docker): Run Ze in a Docker container for evaluation, lab testing, or lightweight deployments where you don't need interface configuration or kernel-level features (VPP, L2TP, nftables).
- [netlab](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/netlab): netlab builds a lab from a short YAML topology and starts each node under containerlab.
- [Appliance](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/appliance): Ze ships a bootable VM appliance image: a minimal Linux system built with gokrazy that runs Ze as its only application.
- [Quick Start](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/quick-start): You have a built ze binary.
- [ExaBGP Migration](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/exabgp-migration): This is the first page to read if you already run ExaBGP.
- [CLI Tour](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/cli-tour): The Ze CLI is a network-OS shell, not a Unix CLI bolted on top of a daemon.
- [Web UI Tour](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/web-ui-tour): The web UI is the same engine as the CLI with a different surface on top.

### Configuration

- [Configuration](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/configuration): This is the configuration section.
- [Overview](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/overview): Configuration in Ze is one tree, validated by one set of YANG schemas, edited from any of the five operator surfaces (CLI, web UI, Looking Glass, MCP, REST API), committed atomically, and rolled back...
- [YANG Model](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/yang-model): Every field in Ze comes from a YANG schema.
- [Editor Workflow](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/editor-workflow): The config editor is the piece of Ze that turns "edit a text file and hope" into the network-OS workflow operators actually expect.
- [Archive and Rollback](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/archive-and-rollback): Every committed configuration in Ze is kept.
- [System](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/system): The system { } block carries the identity of the Ze instance and the global settings that do not belong to a specific subsystem.
- [Interfaces](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/configuration-interfaces): Ze manages Linux network interfaces through the iface component, backed by pure netlink.
- [VRRP](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/vrrp): VRRP gives a LAN a gateway address that survives the loss of the router holding it.
- [BFD](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bfd): Ze includes a full BFD implementation (RFC 5880/5881/5882/5883) as a plugin.
- [FIB](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/fib): The FIB pipeline in Ze takes BGP best-path output and programs the forwarding table.
- [OSPF](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/ospf): Ze includes an experimental native OSPF engine under the ospf config root.
- [IS-IS](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/isis): Ze implements IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System, ISO/IEC 10589 as updated by RFC 1195 / RFC 5305 / RFC 5308 / RFC 5301) as a native link-state interior gateway protocol that runs...
- [MPLS / LDP / RSVP-TE](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/mpls): Ze can act as a Linux MPLS label-switching router (LSR).
- [RSVP-TE](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/rsvp-te): RSVP-TE (RFC 3209, on top of RFC 2205 RSVP) signals explicitly-routed MPLS LSP tunnels with bandwidth reservation.
- [SRv6](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/srv6): SRv6 (Segment Routing over IPv6) Prefix-SID support (RFC 8669, RFC 9252).
- [Static Routes](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/static-routes): Ze supports static routes with ECMP, weighted load balancing, BFD-tracked failover, blackhole, and reject.
- [Policy Routing](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/policy-routing): Ze supports policy-based routing (PBR) to steer traffic through alternate routing tables or next-hops based on L3/L4 match criteria.
- [Firewall](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/firewall): Ze manages nftables packet filter and NAT rules from a single firewall { } YANG section.
- [Traffic Control](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/traffic-control): Ze programs per-interface queueing disciplines, classes, and filters from a single traffic { control { } } YANG section.
- [Class of Service](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/class-of-service): Class-of-Service (CoS) in Ze maps the 3-bit IEEE 802.1p Priority Code Point (PCP) in 802.1Q VLAN headers to internal priorities and back.
- [L2TP/PPP](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/l2tp): Ze includes a native L2TPv2 (RFC 2661) LNS/LAC implementation for use as a BNG (Broadband Network Gateway) component.
- [PPPoE](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/pppoe): Ze implements an RFC 2516 PPPoE access concentrator for direct-attach subscriber access.
- [VPP Data Plane](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/vpp): Ze optionally integrates with VPP (the FD.io Vector Packet Processor) to forward packets at DPDK speed.
- [RPKI](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/rpki): Ze validates received BGP routes against RPKI ROA data.
- [IPsec VPN](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/ipsec): Ze implements native IKEv2 in Go for route-based IPsec VPN tunnels.
- [TACACS+ AAA](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/tacacs): Ze authenticates SSH logins against TACACS+ servers (RFC 8907) when the system.authentication.tacacs block is present.
- [RADIUS AAA](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/radius): Ze authenticates operator logins (SSH, web, MCP) against RADIUS servers (RFC 2865) when the system.authentication.radius block is present.
- [AS112 DNS](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/as112): Ze's as112 plugin runs an AS112 anycast DNS node: an authoritative sink for misdirected reverse-DNS queries about RFC 1918 and link-local address space (RFC 7534), plus the EMPTY.AS112.ARPA...
- [DNS](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/dns): Ze is on both sides of DNS.
- [Authorization](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/authorization): Ze supports profile-based command authorization.
- [Fleet](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/fleet): Fleet mode is Ze's answer to "I have 20 boxes and I want to manage their config from one place".
- [BGP](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/configuration-bgp): The BGP subtree of the config.
- [Peers](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/peers): A BGP peer in Ze is a named entry under bgp { peer <name> { } }.
- [Policies](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/policies): Ze does not have a built-in filter language in the style of BIRD's filter DSL or FRR's route-map.
- [Address Families](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/address-families): Address families in Ze fall into two groups.
- [ADD-PATH](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/add-path): ADD-PATH (RFC 7911) lets BGP advertise more than one path per prefix by prefixing each NLRI with a 4-byte Path Identifier.
- [Graceful Restart](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/graceful-restart): Graceful Restart (RFC 4724) and Long-Lived Graceful Restart (RFC 9494) let a BGP session preserve forwarding state across a restart of one side, instead of dropping every route and waiting for...
- [BGP Role](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/configuration-bgp-role): BGP Role (RFC 9234) prevents route leaks by declaring the business relationship between peers.
- [Route Reflection](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/route-reflection): Ze operates as both a route server (RFC 7947) and an iBGP route reflector (RFC 4456).
- [Route Injection](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/route-injection): Route injection is one of the two things Ze was built for.
- [Route Filters](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/redistribution): Route filters let plugins act on BGP UPDATEs as they move through the daemon.

### Operation

- [Operation](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/operation): This section is for the day-2 operator.
- [Starting and Stopping](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/starting-and-stopping): Running Ze is the same as running any other Unix daemon with one small twist: SSH credentials must exist before the daemon can expose its CLI.
- [Show Commands](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/show-commands): This is the day-2 operator's quick reference for the ze show family.
- [Monitoring](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/monitoring): Ze gives you three different ways to watch a running daemon: an auto-refreshing peer dashboard for the operator at the keyboard, a live event stream for the engineer chasing a bug, and a Prometheus...
- [Flow Export](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/flow-export): Ze exports interface counters and per-flow records to external collectors over UDP.
- [DDoS Mitigation](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/ddos): Ze can automatically detect volumetric DDoS attacks on its interfaces, mitigate them on the host or upstream, and report incidents to the Flowtriq cloud.
- [Anomaly Detection](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/anomaly): Ze has a behavioral anomaly detector: a report-only subsystem that builds a per-source behavioral baseline, scores how far each source deviates from its own history and from its peers, and correlates...
- [Health Checks](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/health-checks): Ze provides two complementary systems for monitoring operational health: offline doctor checks (pre-start readiness) and runtime health monitoring (continuous anomaly detection during operation).
- [Audit Trail](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/audit): Ze keeps a local structured audit log for operator actions that change state or fail authentication.
- [Production Diagnostics](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/production-diagnostics): Symptom-based troubleshooting using Ze's built-in diagnostic commands.
- [Logging](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/logging): Ze uses hierarchical, structured logging with runtime-configurable levels per subsystem.
- [Operational Reports](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/operational-reports): Ze has a single bus for operator-visible issues, backed by two CLI commands: ze show warnings and ze show errors.
- [Healthcheck](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/healthcheck): The Ze healthcheck monitors a service by running a shell command on a timer and controls BGP route announcement or withdrawal through a watchdog group.
- [Self-Update](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/self-update): Ze can automatically download, verify, and install firmware updates on non-gokrazy deployments.
- [Zero-Touch Provisioning](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/ze-install): ze install remote is a one-command, zero-touch provisioning (ZTP) server that PXE-boots target machines with a gokrazy appliance image containing Ze.
- [MRT Analysis](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/mrt-analysis): Ze provides both daemon-side MRT recording and a standalone analysis tool.
- [Upgrade and Restart](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/upgrade-and-restart): The point of this page is one thing: how to replace the binary, reload the config, or restart the daemon without dropping your BGP sessions or black-holing traffic.

### Interfaces

- [Interfaces](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/interfaces): Ze exposes the same engine through five different surfaces.
- [CLI](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/cli): The CLI is a network OS shell, not a Unix wrapper.
- [Web UI](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/web-ui): The web UI is the same engine as the CLI with a different surface.
- [Looking Glass](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/looking-glass): The Looking Glass is the public, read-only side of Ze.
- [MCP](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/mcp): The MCP server is the surface you use when an AI assistant should drive Ze.
- [REST API](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/rest-api): The REST API is Ze's programmatic HTTP surface for running commands and editing configuration from anywhere that can speak JSON.
- [gRPC API](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/grpc-api): The gRPC API is the typed-RPC counterpart to the REST API.
- [gNMI](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/gnmi): Ze includes a gNMI (gRPC Network Management Interface) server that exposes the YANG-modeled configuration over the industry-standard gNMI protocol.
- [Introspection](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/introspection): Ze is self-documenting.

### Plugins

- [Plugins](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/plugins): A plugin in Ze is a unit of behaviour that registers itself with the engine and reacts to events on the bus.
- [bgp-rib](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-rib): The main BGP RIB store and best-path selection engine.
- [bgp-adj-rib-in](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-adj-rib-in): Per-peer Adj-RIB-In store with raw hex replay for forensic analysis and route server convergence.
- [bgp-persist](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-persist): In-memory sent-route cache with replay on peer reconnect.
- [bgp-rs](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-rs): RFC 7947 route server: forwards every received route to every other peer, with zero-copy wire forwarding when peers share an encoding context.
- [bgp-rr](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-rr): RFC 4456 iBGP route reflector.
- [bgp-filter-community](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-filter-community): Community filter plugin for tagging, stripping, and matching communities (standard, large, extended) on ingress and egress.
- [bgp-filter-prefix](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-filter-prefix): Named prefix-list filter (CIDR + ge/le + accept/reject).
- [bgp-filter-aspath](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-filter-aspath): Named AS-path regex filter (ordered entries, first match wins, accept/reject).
- [bgp-route-modify](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-route-modify): Named route attribute modifier.
- [bgp-filter-irr](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-filter-irr): The bgp-filter-irr plugin filters incoming BGP routes against prefix lists derived from Internet Routing Registry (IRR) data.
- [bgp-redistribute](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-redistribute): Cross-protocol route redistribution.
- [bgp-role](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-role): RFC 9234 BGP Role enforcement.
- [bgp](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp): The core BGP plugin implementing RFC 4271.
- [bgp-healthcheck](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-healthcheck): Service healthcheck plugin with watchdog route control.
- [interface](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/interface): OS network interface monitoring and management.
- [loop](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/loop): Route loop detection ingress filter per RFC 4271 Section 9 and RFC 4456 Section 8.
- [bgp-gr](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-gr): Graceful Restart (RFC 4724) and Long-Lived Graceful Restart (RFC 9494) state machine.
- [bgp-watchdog](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-watchdog): Deferred route announcement controlled by named watchdog groups.
- [bgp-route-refresh](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-route-refresh): Route Refresh (RFC 2918) and Enhanced Route Refresh (RFC 7313).
- [bgp-rpki](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-rpki): RPKI origin validation via the RTR protocol (RFC 6811, RFC 8210) and ASPA path verification with policy enforcement (RTR v2, RFC 9582, draft-ietf-sidrops-aspa-verification).
- [bgp-rpki-decorator](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-rpki-decorator): Correlates UPDATE events and RPKI validation events into merged update-rpki events for consumer plugins that want both in one envelope.
- [bgp-aigp](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-aigp): Accumulated IGP metric (RFC 7311).
- [bgp-hostname](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-hostname): FQDN capability. Advertises the local hostname and fully-qualified domain name to peers in the OPEN message.
- [bgp-llnh](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-llnh): Link-Local Next Hop for IPv6 (RFC 2545).
- [bgp-softver](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-softver): Software version capability.
- [bgp-nlri-vpn](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-nlri-vpn): MPLS-VPN address families: IPv4 VPN (AFI 1 / SAFI 128) and IPv6 VPN (AFI 2 / SAFI 128), per RFC 4364.
- [bgp-nlri-evpn](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-nlri-evpn): L2VPN EVPN (AFI 25 / SAFI 70), per RFC 7432.
- [bgp-nlri-flowspec](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-nlri-flowspec): BGP FlowSpec (RFC 8955, RFC 8956) for IPv4 and IPv6, plus the VPN variants.
- [bgp-nlri-ls](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-nlri-ls): BGP Link-State (RFC 7752) and its VPN variant.
- [bgp-nlri-labeled](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-nlri-labeled): MPLS labelled unicast for IPv4 (AFI 1 / SAFI 4) and IPv6 (AFI 2 / SAFI 4).
- [bgp-nlri-vpls](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-nlri-vpls): L2VPN VPLS (AFI 25 / SAFI 65), RFC 4761 / RFC 4762.
- [bgp-nlri-mvpn](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-nlri-mvpn): Multicast VPN (RFC 6513, RFC 6514) for IPv4 (AFI 1 / SAFI 5) and IPv6 (AFI 2 / SAFI 5).
- [bgp-nlri-rtc](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-nlri-rtc): Route Target Constrain (RFC 4684).
- [bgp-nlri-mup](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-nlri-mup): Mobile User Plane SAFI for IPv4 (AFI 1 / SAFI 85) and IPv6 (AFI 2 / SAFI 85).
- [bgp-nlri-srpolicy](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bgp-nlri-srpolicy): SR-Policy NLRI (SAFI 73, RFC 9830) carries Segment Routing policy information over BGP.
- [bgp-bmp](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/bmp): Ze implements RFC 7854 BMP in both directions: as a receiver (accepting feeds from routers) and as a sender (streaming state to collectors).
- [ntp](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/ntp): Ze includes an NTP client plugin for system clock synchronization.
- [sysctl](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/sysctl): Ze includes a sysctl plugin that manages kernel parameters with named profiles.
- [dhcp-server](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/dhcp-server): DHCP server plugin serving leases to LAN clients per RFC 2131/2132.
- [fib-kernel](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/fib-kernel): Programs the Linux kernel forwarding table via netlink.
- [fib-p4](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/fib-p4): Experimental P4 dataplane backend.
- [iface-dhcp](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/iface-dhcp): DHCP client for managed interfaces.
- [iface-netlink](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/iface-netlink): Netlink backend for the iface component.
- [sysrib](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/sysrib): Cross-protocol RIB selector.
- [host](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/host-inventory): The host inventory plugin provides hardware detection, SMART health monitoring, and a hardware tuning engine.

### Plugin Development

- [Plugin Development](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/plugin-development): This is the plugin author's section.
- [Go Plugins](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/go-plugins): This page is the five-minute version of writing a Go plugin against the Ze SDK.
- [External Plugins](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/external-plugins): An external plugin is a separate process.
- [YANG Schema](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/yang-schema): Every plugin that has its own configuration ships a YANG schema.
- [Handlers](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/handlers): Handlers are the callbacks a plugin registers with the SDK to react to engine-initiated events.
- [Commands](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/commands): A plugin exposes commands by declaring them in its Registration at startup and handling them with OnExecuteCommand at runtime.
- [Testing](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/plugin-testing): The Ze plugin SDK is designed to be testable.

### Chaos Testing

- [Chaos Testing](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/chaos-testing): Chaos testing is built into Ze.
- [Scenarios](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/scenarios): A chaos scenario in Ze is a configuration of ze-chaos: the number of mock peers, the address families they negotiate, the duration, the chaos seed and rate, and any explicit fault triggers.
- [Dashboard](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/dashboard): The chaos dashboard is a live web UI for ze-chaos.
- [Property Verification](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/property-verification): Property verification is the part of ze-chaos that turns "did the run finish without crashing" into something useful.

### Blueprints

- [Blueprints](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/blueprints): Blueprints are end-to-end worked examples.
- [Route Server at an IXP](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/route-server-at-an-ixp): Running Ze as an IXP route server.
- [Transit Edge with RPKI](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/transit-edge-with-rpki): A transit customer edge router.
- [Public Looking Glass](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/public-looking-glass): Stand up a public Looking Glass for your AS.
- [ExaBGP Migration Walkthrough](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/exabgp-migration-walkthrough): A complete worked migration of a non-trivial ExaBGP setup to Ze.
- [FlowSpec Injection](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/flowspec-injection): Inject BGP FlowSpec rules from a script for DDoS mitigation.
- [Chaos-Tested Peering](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/chaos-tested-peering): Set up a peering session and verify that it survives a battery of chaos scenarios.
- [AS Path Topology](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/as-path-topology): Use the Looking Glass topology graph to visualise a real network's AS paths.

### Development

- [Development](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/development): This is the developer's section.
- [Building](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/building): Building Ze from source is a single command if you have Go 1.26 and a working toolchain on the path.
- [Repo Layout](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/repo-layout): The Ze repo is organised around three top-level Go directories (cmd/, internal/, pkg/) and a set of supporting directories for docs, tests, schemas, and tooling.
- [Coding Standards](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/coding-standards): Ze has a set of coding rules that apply to every contribution, whether you write the code by hand or with AI assistance.
- [Testing](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/testing): Ze has five test suites: unit, functional, fuzz, chaos, and mutation.
- [Debugging](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/debugging): Debugging Ze is mostly a matter of knowing which tool to reach for.
- [CI](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/ci): Ze's CI runs the same Make targets that you run locally, so that "works locally" and "passes CI" are the same statement.
- [RFC Compliance](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/rfc-implementation): Ze implements a lot of standards documents.
- [Contributing](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/contributing): Contributions to Ze are welcome.
- [Claude Code](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/claude-code): Ze is developed with Claude Code, and the repo ships a set of project-specific slash commands under .claude/skills/.
- [Performance](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/performance): ze-perf is a BGP propagation latency benchmark tool.
- [Mock Servers](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/mock-servers): ze-test is the test harness for Ze.

### Reference

- [Reference](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/reference): The reference section is where you look when you need an exact answer.
- [Command Reference](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/command-reference): Ze commands fall into two categories.
- [Feature Inventory](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/feature-inventory): The full inventory of what Ze does.
- [Comparison](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/comparison): This page summarises how Ze lines up against the other open-source BGP daemons.
- [Configuration Reference](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/configuration-reference): The exact shape of every configuration field in Ze lives in the YANG schemas themselves, not in a separately-maintained reference.
- [Deprecated Options](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/deprecated-options): Configuration syntax that used to work and no longer does, with the migration path for each.
- [Glossary](https://github.com/ze-software/ze/wiki/glossary): Terms and acronyms that appear throughout the Ze documentation.
